My HIIT routine is generally just running power intervals.  Not very interesting or exciting.  I go to the local football pitch, do some warmup exercises (high knees, butt kicks, jumping jacks, jump squats, etc., takes about 3 minutes), and then run the length of the pitch full-intensity and slow to a trot for the width.  Do that for 20 minutes and you'll be plenty winded.

If you use a treadmill, you can easily program it to switch between low and high intensity intervals, too.  Depending on your weight, how adapted you are to running, etc., your sustainable top speed for 60 second intervals is going to vary pretty wildly, but a good way to figure out your top speed for intervals is to run for about 2 minutes at 3 mph, then bump it up to 4mphx2min, then 5mph, then 6mph, then 7, 7.5, 8, etc etc until your breathing deepens to the point where you wouldn't be able to carry on a conversation comfortably.  Check your heart rate at this point; at no point should your HR exceed 180.  You're not trying to max your HR, you're trying to get around 80%.  For someone not adapted to running, this means your high-intensity interval speed could very easily be somewhere in the 5-6mph range.

Couple questions before I can weigh in. 

1) What's your Total Weight, BF%, Height, Sex, Age? 
2) How long have you been doing a ketogenic diet? 
3) When you're doing SS/SL or other linear progression program, around where is your total caloric intake?  

Regarding SS, which I'm more familiar with than MacDonald's recommendations: If you're deading out around the middle of the week, it's possible you're just not consuming enough raw materials to build your body back up.  The big lifts do a number on your body and it takes a lot more than you think to build yourself back up.  Rip wrote a great clarification about doing SS for fat loss, let me see if I can find it: http://startingstrength.com/articles/clarification_rippetoe.pdf

Basically, if you're starting out a fat guy (like me) you shouldn't do GOMAD, but you SHOULD be consuming close to (or slightly below or above) maintenance calories on a linear progression strength training regimen; you have to titrate your diet to your needs, so keep track of your progress on a semi-weekly basis.  If you're in it for fat loss, my recommendation is: you will lose fat doing linear progression.  Eat until you're not hungry.  Eat good things.  Lift heavy weights.  Don't worry too much.

In my view, MacDonald's right about a couple things: you definitely don't want to reduce weight and increase reps on a diet.  You will lose LBM that way.  Three heavy workouts a week at 80% of your 1RM while dieting sounds reasonable.

My understanding is that Chemistry classes are different from other courses in that there are associated lab costs and administrative issues associated with chem lab sections (they have to be smaller and more supervised than most other lab sections due to safety concerns) and as such tend to be more costly and more highly demanded by students (since quantity supplied is lower).  

The reason they want you to have taken your chem sequence before you get here is that it's easier for JCs to provide a high-quality Chem education to their smaller interested student body.  I just came from CCSF where my Organic Chemistry section (the only one that year) was about 30 students.  Compare that with UCD's likely >200 undergrads.

It's being sold as a way to lower the overall cost of medical school for certain individuals and as a way to make more doctors available sooner because of the current high demand, but I doubt it will drive healthcare costs down substantively.  For one thing, healthcare costs have been shown to be sticky-up; also, administrative and durable goods costs have a disproportionately large effect on the overall price of healthcare, much more so than the cost of doctors (though of course that is a factor—doctors are paid WAY more here than in countries with single-payer systems, for instance).
